analysis.investment_thesis: Indian Overseas Bank is a government-owned PSU bank where the promoter holds 92.44% — meaning capital allocation is driven by New Delhi, not economics. With ROE of 11.4%, a forward P/E of 38.8x (implying earnings will collapse from current levels), and a structural inability to compete on talent or technology with private banks, this is a business I would not own at any price.
key_strengths: Profits have grown from INR 758 Cr (FY21) to INR 3,396 Cr (FY25), reflecting resolution of the massive NPA crisis that plagued PSU banks for years
P/B of 1.97x and P/E of 13.6x trailing appear surface-level reasonable for a bank that is finally profitable
Large branch network and government backing provides implicit liquidity support that private peers lack
key_risks: Forward P/E of 38.8x vs trailing 13.6x is a catastrophic red flag — analysts expect FY26 earnings to fall precipitously, likely due to credit costs normalising upward
ROE of 11.4% is structurally inadequate for a bank; private sector peers earn 15-20%+ ROE with better technology, lower cost-to-income, and no political lending mandates
Government ownership at 92.44% means management cannot make optimal capital allocation decisions — directed lending, employee expansion, and recapitalisation are all politically driven
red_flags: Forward P/E of 38.84 against trailing P/E of 13.6 — this gap implies a ~60% earnings decline is expected, making the stock far more expensive than it appears
OCF was deeply negative in FY23 (-INR 13,655 Cr) and FY24 (-INR 1,119 Cr) — banking OCF is noisy but sustained negative OCF indicates aggressive loan book expansion funded by borrowed money
Total debt jumped from INR 20,804 Cr (2023) to INR 40,282 Cr (2025) — a near-doubling of borrowings in two years signals rapid balance sheet expansion that could mask deteriorating asset quality
analysis.detailed_analysis:
I have always avoided government-owned enterprises. The chairman of a PSU bank answers to a minister, not to shareholders. Staffing, branch expansion, agricultural loan waivers — none of these decisions are made by asking 'what generates the best return on equity?' IOB's ROE of 11.4% confirms this: a decade of reforms and this is the best they can deliver in a good credit cycle. When the cycle turns, the government will need to recapitalise again.

The forward P/E discrepancy is perhaps the most alarming data point in this entire set of five stocks. The market is pricing in a near-collapse of earnings in FY26 — if that is correct, then the stock trading at INR 35 is not cheap at all. If it is wrong, the bank is still a mediocre compounder at best. Either way, I see no case for ownership.
